```{=html}
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Simulated panels with known effects: what each estimate says</p>
<ol><li>Simulated: 400 homes, 24 months; 92 opted into a time-of-use tariff from month 13. The true effect on them is −0.29 kW on the evening peak (known because the data are simulated).</li>
<li>After the start, TOU homes against flat homes: −0.85 kW. With home size as a control: −0.73 kW. Engagement, never measured, still differs.</li>
<li>TOU homes after against before: −0.36 kW, because flat homes also changed by −0.06 kW (a cooler second summer).</li>
<li>Difference-in-differences: −0.30 kW (about 95% interval −0.33 to −0.27 kW), against the truth −0.29 kW. Before month 13 the change in the TOU–flat gap, against month 12, stays within 0.04 kW of zero.</li>
<li>Threats move it: already cutting −0.44 kW, early cuts −0.26 kW, neighbours copy −0.22 kW, a thermostat offer −0.42 kW.</li>
<li>If every home were put on the tariff by default, the average effect would be −0.20 kW, not −0.29 kW: those who opt in respond more.</li>
<li>Simulated regions: 14 of 30 adopt a policy in 2021. DiD: 10.0 MW a year of new solar per adopting region (truth +10.0); if the policy followed a boom, 22.5 MW a year.</li>
<li>If projects moved across the border, DiD reads 14.0 MW a year. Adopters then gain 140 MW a year: 64 moved from the other regions and 76 is new.</li></ol>
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts m14-fbtab">
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Estimate of the tariff's effect</th><th scope="col">kW</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>Truth (homes that opted in)</td><td class="n">−0.29 kW</td></tr>
<tr><td>Naive after-period gap</td><td class="n">−0.85 kW</td></tr>
<tr><td>Regression with home size</td><td class="n">−0.73 kW</td></tr>
<tr><td>Before against after, TOU homes only</td><td class="n">−0.36 kW</td></tr>
<tr><td>Difference-in-differences</td><td class="n">−0.30 kW</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>

</div>
</div>
```

::: {#explain .lx-sec}
::: {.lx-sec-h}
## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="m14-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Counterfactual</dt><dd>An effect is a comparison with what would have happened without the change; it is never observed.</dd>
<dt>Selection</dt><dd>People who choose a programme differ from those who do not, before it starts.</dd>
<dt>Difference-in-differences</dt><dd>Compare the change in the treated group with the change in a comparison group.</dd>
<dt>Parallel trends</dt><dd>The assumption that both groups would have moved alike; the months before can make it plausible, never prove it.</dd>
<dt>Threats</dt><dd>Selection on trends, confounding, spillovers and anticipation each move the estimate away from the truth.</dd>
<dt>For whom</dt><dd>An effect on volunteers is not the effect on everyone.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The formulas: DiD, the two-way regression, the event study and standard errors</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $i$, $t$ | a home; a month, 1 to 24 (the tariff starts in month 13) |
| $y_{it}$ | home $i$'s evening peak in month $t$, kW |
| $D_{it}$ | 1 if home $i$ is on the tariff in month $t$, else 0 |
| $\mathbf{1}[\cdot]$ | 1 when the condition in the brackets holds, else 0 |
| $\tau$ | the tariff's effect, kW |
| $\alpha_i$, $\lambda_t$ | one level for each home; one level for each month |
| $\varepsilon_{it}$ | what the model leaves unexplained (noise), kW |
| $\bar y_{T,\text{post}}$ | the mean over TOU homes ($T$) in months 13 to 24 (post); $C$ flat homes, pre months 1 to 12 |
| $n_T$, $n_C$ | the numbers of TOU and flat homes: 92 and 308 |
| $\Delta_i$, $s_T^2$, $s_C^2$ | home $i$'s change, after minus before; the variance of the changes in each group |
| $\beta_k$, $k$ | the change in the gap $k$ months from the start ($k = t - 13$) |

- **DiD of means.** $\hat\tau = (\bar y_{T,\text{post}} - \bar y_{T,\text{pre}}) - (\bar y_{C,\text{post}} - \bar y_{C,\text{pre}})$. On this page: $-0.36 - (-0.06) = -0.30$ kW (rounded).
- **Two-way fixed effects.** $y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \tau D_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}$, one level $\alpha_i$ per home and one $\lambda_t$ per month. With one start date and every home seen every month, its $\hat\tau$ equals the DiD of means; the lab checks this.
- **Event study.** Replace $\tau D_{it}$ by $\sum_{k \ne -1} \beta_k \,\mathbf{1}[\text{TOU}_i,\ t - 13 = k]$. Before the start ($k < -1$) the $\beta_k$ should sit near zero.
- **Computed or fitted.** With one start date and every home seen every month, each $\beta_k$ equals that month's DiD against month 12. The page computes it that way; the lab fits the regression and checks that the two agree.
- **Standard error.** $\text{SE} = \sqrt{s_T^2/n_T + s_C^2/n_C}$, from each home's change $\Delta_i = \bar y_{i,\text{post}} - \bar y_{i,\text{pre}}$.
- **Clustering.** A home's months are not independent, so the home, not the month, is the unit: this is what clustering by home does in the regression.
- **Interval.** Estimate ± 1.96 SE: about 95% of such intervals hold the truth when the design's assumptions hold ([K5](k05-probability-statistics.html)). When they fail, a narrow interval misses: step 7.
- **Start dates that differ.** When units start at different dates, the two-way regression mixes comparisons, some of them against units already treated. Goodman-Bacon (2021) and Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021) set out the problem and estimators for it (Sources).

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Researcher</span>Randomized trials and natural experiments</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Randomized trial.** Chance decides who gets the tariff, so the groups differ only by chance before the start. DOE's consumer behaviour studies used randomized designs for this reason (Sources).
- **Randomized encouragement.** When people cannot be forced onto a tariff, chance decides who is invited or defaulted; the comparison is between the invited and the not invited.
- **Natural experiment.** An outside rule or event creates a comparison: a start date by postcode, a threshold, a border. For DiD, explain why the untreated trends would have matched, and check for anticipation, spillovers and other changes at the same time.
- **Pre-register.** Write the comparison, the outcome and the threats down before looking at the after-period data.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="m14-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="controls" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Add enough control variables and a regression gives the causal effect.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Controls fix only measured differences. On this page home size and air conditioning moved the estimate from −0.85 to −0.70 kW; the truth was −0.29 kW, and engagement was never measured.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="pretrend" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Flat months before the start prove the DiD estimate is right.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. With neighbours copying or a thermostat offer, the months before stayed flat while DiD read −0.22 and −0.42 kW against a truth of −0.29. Similar earlier trends support a comparison; they never prove it.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="volunteers" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “An effect measured on volunteers tells you the effect of making the tariff everyone's default.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Here volunteers cut 0.29 kW, the average home would cut 0.20. DOE's studies reported peak cuts of 12% for opt-in TOU customers and 6% for opt-out (2016).</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="m14">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="did" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">Treated homes' peak fell from 2.00 to 1.70 kW; comparison homes' from 2.10 to 2.00 kW. The DiD estimate?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">−0.30 kW</li><li data-value="b">−0.20 kW</li><li data-value="c">−0.10 kW</li><li data-value="d">−0.30 kW minus the 0.10 kW gap at the start</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>−0.20 kW: (1.70 − 2.00) − (2.00 − 2.10) = −0.30 + 0.10.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="spill" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">A city's subsidy moves solar projects from the next county into the city. A DiD with that county as the comparison…</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">is unbiased, since the county had no subsidy</li><li data-value="b">understates the city's gain</li><li data-value="c">overstates the net gain across both</li><li data-value="d">cannot be computed</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>It overstates it: the county lost projects, so the comparison group falls and the gap grows. The net change across both is smaller (step 9).</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Where this came up in practice</p>
<p>Under the Smart Grid Investment Grant, ten utilities ran eleven consumer behaviour studies of time-based rates, applying randomized and controlled designs to estimate customers' responses more precisely and credibly (DOE, November 2016, pp. iv–v).</p>
<p>Opt-out enrolment was far higher than opt-in (92% against 15%), peak-period cuts were generally lower (6% against 12% for TOU), and retention was about the same (90% against 87%) (p. vi).</p>
<p><b>A selection example</b> (same report, Table ES-2, p. viii): in one utility's opt-in TOU study, homes with in-home displays cut their peak somewhat more than homes without.</p>
<p>The report says pre-treatment differences between the two groups can explain that gap.</p>
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-sources">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Sources and further reading</p>
<ul>
<li>U.S. Department of Energy, Smart Grid Investment Grant Program (2016). <a href="https://www.energy.gov/sites/prod/files/2017/01/f34/CBS_Final_Program_Impact_Report_20161107.pdf">Final Report on Customer Acceptance, Retention, and Response to Time-Based Rates from the Consumer Behavior Studies</a> (PDF), November 2016: executive summary, pp. iv–viii (accessed 6 Nov 2026).</li>
<li>Goodman-Bacon, A. (2021). <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2021.03.014">Difference-in-differences with variation in treatment timing</a>. <em>Journal of Econometrics</em>, 225(2), 254–277.</li>
<li>Callaway, B., and Sant'Anna, P. H. C. (2021). <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2020.12.001">Difference-in-Differences with multiple time periods</a>. <em>Journal of Econometrics</em>, 225(2), 200–230.</li>
<li>Further reading (free online textbooks, by name): Cunningham, S., <em>Causal Inference: The Mixtape</em> (2021); Huntington-Klein, N., <em>The Effect</em> (2021), chapters on difference-in-differences and event studies.</li>
</ul>
</div>
```
